In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: al-humaza is one who eats the flesh of people and backbites them, and al-lumaza is one who defames them. Mujahid said: al-humaza is one who attacks people, and al-lumaza is one who attacks people's lineages. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 30/375.]

Abu al-'Aliyya, al-Hasan and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: al-humaza is one who speaks ill of a man in his absence and attacks his face when he comes, while al-lumaza is one who backbites him from behind when he turns away and is absent. Muqatil held the opposite. Murra said: it means every one who attacks and reviles, who backbites a person when he is absent. The evidence is the verse of Ziyad ibn al-A'jam:

"When I meet you from afar, you smile at me,
but when I am absent, you become the one who insults and defames."
[Lisan al-'Arab: 5/426; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 20/182, at the verse.]

Ibn Zayd said: al-humaza is one who strikes people with his hand and beats them, while al-lumaza is one who defames them with his tongue and disparages them.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: he insults with his tongue and defames with his eye. Ibn Kaysan said: al-humaza is one who harms his companion with foul speech, and al-lumaza is one who frowns at his companion, nods with his head, winks with his eye, and signals with his eyebrow. These are two forms for the doer, like sukhara and dahika, for one who mocks and laughs at people.

It is narrated from Abu Ja'far and al-A'raj with the letter mim vowelled with sukun in both words. If this reading is sound, it carries the sense of the passive participle: one who places himself before people when they mock him and laugh at him, and who incites them to backbiting.

'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) and al-A'mash recited: "Woe to the humazah, the lumazah." The root of hamz is to press, to bite down on something forcefully, and from it comes hamz of a letter (the glottal stop). It is related that a Bedouin was asked: "Do you hamz the mouse?" He said: "The cat hamzes it." Al-Hajjaj said:

"And whose head we have hamzed, so it was crushed to pieces."
[Lisan al-'Arab: 5/425.]

The exegetes differed concerning who this verse was revealed about. A group said: it was revealed about Jamil ibn 'Amir al-Jumahi, and Ibn Abi al-Jumah adopted this view. Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Shariq and Wahb ibn 'Amr al-Thaqafi, who used to attack people and backbite them, both to their faces and behind their backs.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar said: "We have always heard that Surat al-Humaza was revealed about Umayyah ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi."

Muqatil said: it was revealed about al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who used to backbite the Prophet (ﷺ) and attack him to his face.

Mujahid and others said: it is not specific to any one person, but applies to everyone who has this characteristic. [See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 20/183.]

﴿Who has gathered wealth and counted it.﴾ Shayba, Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ayyub recited (jama'a) with the mim lightened; Abu Hatim chose this. Others recited it with the mim doubled (jammaʿa); Abu 'Ubayd chose this. There is a difference of transmission from Ya'qub regarding it.

Muqatil said: he prepared it, stored it up, and made it his equipment. al-Hasan recited wa-ʿaddadahu with the doubling lightened (wa-ʿadadahu), which is weak, though similar forms occur in poetry, where when the doubling was brought out, they lightened it. The poet said:

"Patience, O my blamer, you have tested my character:
I am the most generous of people, even if they are stingy."
[al-Sihah: 6/2156.]

﴿He will surely be thrown﴾ — it means he will be cast down and flung. al-Hasan recited la-yunbadhanna with the dual, la-yunbadhani, meaning he and his wealth. ﴿Into the Crushing (al-Hutama).﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what the Crushing is?﴾ ﴿It is the Fire of Allah, kindled,﴾ ﴿which rises over the hearts.﴾ That is, its pain and agony reach the hearts. The meaning of the verse is that it consumes a part of him until it reaches his heart.

Al-Qurazi and al-Kalbi said: ﴿Indeed it will be closed over them﴾: sealed shut, locked. ﴿In extended columns.﴾ The people of Kufa recited 'umad with two dammas, the others with a fatha, and Abu Hatim chose this, based on His saying: ﴿He raised the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾ [Surat al-Ra'd: 2]. Both are plurals of 'amud, like adim and adam, afiq and afq, qadim and qadm. al-Farra' said: Abu 'Ubayd said it is the plural of 'imad, like ihab and ihab and ahab.

They differed about the meaning of the verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: He will place them in columns, and they will be extended with pillars, and chains will be on their necks, and the doors will be sealed shut upon them with them.

Qatadah said: We have been told they are columns in which they will be tormented in the Fire. It was also said: they are columns stretched across its doors [so as to finalise their despair] of it. It was also said: the meaning is ﴿It will be closed over them﴾ with columns; and likewise it is in the reading of 'Abd Allah: "with columns," with the letter ba'. [See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 20/186 for details.]

It is narrated from Anas ibn Malik who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The believer is shrewd, perceptive, cautious, prudent, steadfast, does not hasten, is learned and pious. The hypocrite is a humaza, lumaza, hutama; [he does not stop at doubt nor at what is forbidden], like the firewood-gatherer at night who does not care from where he earns or on what he spends." [In the source: he does not stop at doubt nor at what is forbidden.] [Kanz al-'Ummal: 1/162.]

[Lisan al-'Arab: 5/426; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 20/182, at the verse.]

Ibn Zayd said: al-humaza is one who strikes people with his hand and beats them, while al-lumaza is one who defames them with his tongue and disparages them.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: he insults with his tongue and defames with his eye.
